questions.a: kindness=abstract (cannot touch), flock=collective (one word for a group), Mumbai=proper (specific name, capital), chair=common. A wrong answer calling 'flock' common shows the student missed that one word names the whole group.

questions.q: Is 'strength' abstract or concrete? Defend in one line.
questions.a: Abstract — you cannot touch or weigh strength itself, only its effects. A wrong answer 'concrete because wrestlers have it' reveals the student tests the OWNER not the word.

questions.q: Why is 'rice' usually singular? 'Rices are on the table' — right or wrong?
questions.a: Right answer: wrong — rice is uncountable (a mass, not items); we say 'grains of rice'. A wrong answer accepting 'rices' shows the student pluralizes by habit without checking countability.

questions.q: Nouns sort into families by what they name: common (boy, city), proper (Ravi, Delhi — always ______), collective (team, flock — one word for a group), abstract (honesty, fear — things you cannot touch).

Fill in the blank: Nouns sort into families by what they name: common (boy, city), proper (Ravi, Delhi — always ______), collective (team, flock — one word for a group), abstract (honesty, fear — things you cannot touch).
Fill in the blank: Touch test on the board: can you touch it, see it, weigh it? 'Table' yes → ______. 'Honesty' no → abstract.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student classifies any noun into its family, explains the test for abstract nouns (cannot see/touch/weigh it), and capitalises proper nouns inside sentences.
